name: Baltimore
summary: A port city of rowhouse neighborhoods on the Chesapeake Bay, known for its harbor, Johns Hopkins, steamed crabs and a strong local arts scene.

curated-2026-10.title: Baltimore places and neighborhoods written for Prospero Dungeon
curated-2026-10.note: Well-known public places, institutions and employers from general knowledge. Businesses open and close and rents move: treat this as a snapshot for fiction. Rents are rounded estimates of typical asking ranges, not listings. Coordinates are approximate neighborhood centers.

curated-climate-2026-10.title: Approximate monthly climate for Baltimore (BWI area)
curated-climate-2026-10.note: Rounded values in line with NOAA 1991-2020 normals; refresh with scripts/world when network access to NOAA is available.

neighborhoods.name: Inner Harbor
neighborhoods.summary: The tourist waterfront: promenade, aquarium, science center and harbor views, busy on summer weekends.

neighborhoods.name: Downtown
neighborhoods.summary: Office towers, the stadiums, Lexington Market and the theater district.

neighborhoods.name: Fells Point
neighborhoods.summary: Cobblestone streets, eighteenth-century rowhouses, pubs and live music on the waterfront.

neighborhoods.name: Harbor East
neighborhoods.summary: Polished new towers, hotels, offices and upscale restaurants between downtown and Fells Point.

neighborhoods.name: Little Italy
neighborhoods.summary: A few compact blocks of Italian restaurants, bakeries and bocce, with an outdoor film festival in summer.

neighborhoods.name: Canton
neighborhoods.summary: Former cannery rowhouses turned young-professional hub around O'Donnell Square, with a waterfront park and the marine terminals beyond.

neighborhoods.name: Highlandtown
neighborhoods.summary: Working-class rowhouses beside Patterson Park, with Latin American groceries and an arts district.

neighborhoods.name: Federal Hill
neighborhoods.summary: Hilltop park views over the harbor, a lively bar strip and Cross Street Market.

neighborhoods.name: Locust Point
neighborhoods.summary: A quiet peninsula of rowhouses on the way to Fort McHenry, beside the Domino Sugars plant and its neon sign.

neighborhoods.name: Baltimore Peninsula
neighborhoods.summary: A new mixed-use waterfront district in Port Covington, home to Under Armour's headquarters.

neighborhoods.name: Mount Vernon
neighborhoods.summary: Grand nineteenth-century townhouses around the original Washington Monument, with museums, the Peabody and a strong LGBTQ+ community.

neighborhoods.name: Bolton Hill
neighborhoods.summary: Leafy brick townhouse blocks next to the MICA campus.

neighborhoods.name: Station North
neighborhoods.summary: The arts and entertainment district around Penn Station: murals, studios, an indie cinema and late-night bars.

neighborhoods.name: Remington
neighborhoods.summary: Small rowhouse blocks between Hampden and Charles Village with a food hall and music venues.

neighborhoods.name: Charles Village
neighborhoods.summary: Painted Ladies rowhouses around the Johns Hopkins Homewood campus and the Baltimore Museum of Art.

neighborhoods.name: Hampden
neighborhoods.summary: Former mill village turned quirky shopping strip on 36th Street ("The Avenue"), with thrift shops, cafes and a famous Christmas light block.

neighborhoods.name: Reservoir Hill
neighborhoods.summary: Large Victorian homes on the edge of Druid Hill Park and the Maryland Zoo.

neighborhoods.name: Roland Park
neighborhoods.summary: One of the first planned suburbs in the country: winding streets, large houses, private schools and old trees.

neighborhoods.name: Lauraville
neighborhoods.summary: Northeast Baltimore single-family homes with porches near Morgan State and the Harford Road restaurant strip.

neighborhoods.name: Towson
neighborhoods.summary: The Baltimore County seat just north of the city: Towson University, a large mall, hospitals and a busy suburban downtown.

neighborhoods.name: East Baltimore Midway
neighborhoods.summary: The neighborhood around the Johns Hopkins medical campus, with new graduate housing beside older rowhouse blocks.

transit.name: Light RailLink

transit.name: Metro SubwayLink
transit.summary: A single line from Owings Mills through downtown to Johns Hopkins Hospital.

transit.name: CityLink and LocalLink buses
transit.summary: The MTA bus network, the main way around for people without cars.

transit.name: Charm City Circulator
transit.summary: Free downtown buses linking the harbor, Fells Point, Federal Hill, Mount Vernon and Penn Station.

transit.name: Baltimore Water Taxi
transit.summary: Harbor boats between the Inner Harbor, Fells Point, Canton, Harbor East, Locust Point and Fort McHenry.

transit.name: MARC Penn Line
transit.summary: Commuter trains from Penn Station to Washington, D.C., used by many federal workers.

local_color.name: Steamed blue crabs
local_color.summary: Chesapeake blue crabs steamed with a crust of Old Bay-style seasoning, tipped onto brown paper and picked at with mallets and knives over pitchers of beer; they are heaviest and best in late summer and early fall.

local_color.name: Crab cake
local_color.summary: A Maryland crab cake is mostly jumbo lump crab with just enough binder to hold it, broiled or fried and eaten on a platter or with saltines; locals argue hard about filler.

local_color.name: Soft-shell crab sandwich
local_color.summary: Blue crabs caught just after molting are fried whole, legs and all, and served on white bread with lettuce, tomato and tartar sauce.

local_color.name: Old Bay on everything
local_color.summary: Old Bay seasoning was created in Baltimore, and locals shake it on fries, corn, popcorn, chicken wings and the rims of Bloody Marys, not just crabs.

local_color.name: Pit beef
local_color.summary: Top round charred over charcoal, sliced thin and rare onto a kaiser roll with raw onion and horseradish sauce; the classic stands line Pulaski Highway on the east side.

local_color.name: Berger cookies
local_color.summary: Soft, cakey shortbread cookies buried under a thick layer of fudge icing, sold in grocery stores all over town and brought to every office party.

local_color.name: Lake trout
local_color.summary: A carryout staple that is not trout at all: fried whiting on white bread with hot sauce, sold by the box at corner carryouts.

local_color.name: Snowball
local_color.summary: Finely shaved ice soaked in syrup, with egg custard the local favorite and marshmallow cream on top, sold from neighborhood stands that open for the warm months.

local_color.name: Natty Boh
local_color.summary: National Bohemian, the cheap local lager whose one-eyed, mustachioed Mr. Boh still turns up on signs, T-shirts and bar taps; ordering one is a statement of loyalty.

local_color.name: Half-and-half
local_color.summary: Iced tea mixed with lemonade, bought by the bottle or the styrofoam cup at carryouts and corner stores.

local_color.name: "Hon"
local_color.summary: A friendly "hon" (short for honey) from a waitress or neighbor is classic Baltimore, celebrated with beehive hairdos and cat-eye glasses at Hampden's summer HonFest.

local_color.name: "Goin' downy ocean"
local_color.summary: Baltimorese for heading to Ocean City on the Atlantic for the weekend or the week, the default summer trip; the city name itself comes out as "Bawlmer".

local_color.name: The "O!" in the anthem
local_color.summary: At Orioles games, and many other events in town, the crowd shouts "O!" at "Oh, say does that star-spangled banner yet wave".

local_color.name: Painted window screens
local_color.summary: East Baltimore rowhouses have a tradition of painted window and door screens, usually a cottage-and-stream scene, that lets residents see out while passers-by see only the picture.

local_color.name: Scrubbed marble steps
local_color.summary: Rowhouse front steps are often white marble, and older residents still scrub them on a Saturday morning as a point of pride.

local_color.name: Arabbers
local_color.summary: Street vendors who sell fruit and vegetables from brightly painted horse-drawn carts with jingling bells and sung calls, a tradition that survives in a few West Baltimore stables.

local_color.name: Public markets
local_color.summary: Baltimore still has a network of city public markets where stalls sell crab cakes, deli sandwiches, produce and lunch counter food under one roof.

local_color.name: Crab houses
local_color.summary: Paper-covered tables, mallets, rolls of paper towels and crabs sold by the dozen, priced by size and season.

local_color.name: Baltimore Orioles
local_color.summary: The city's Major League Baseball team plays at Oriole Park at Camden Yards; fans wear orange and black, and Opening Day is an unofficial city holiday.

local_color.name: Baltimore Ravens
local_color.summary: The NFL team, named for Poe's poem, plays at M&T Bank Stadium; Purple Friday sees the whole city wear purple before game days.
